To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the T-type channel CaV3.1 is sensitive to protons and that extracellular Ca2+, which binds to the channel, inhibits this sensitivity.

extracellular acidification induces positive shift of the voltage-dependent activation of CaV3.1 and a shift in channel selectivity toward monvalent cations and these effects are counteracted by extracellular Ca(2+) ions.
extracellular Ca2+, Na+, and protons compete for binding to surface charge sites, to the selectivity-filter region of the channel, and to intermediate closed states in a voltage-dependent manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of extracellular pH on gating and selectivity of T-type Ca2+-channels and the modulation of these effects by extracellular Ca+2 and Na+.
the effects of proton and calcium ions on the T-type calcium channel α1G.
the modulation by extracelullar calcium on the effects of extracelullary protons on the gating and conduction properties of the low voltage-activated calcium channel α1G.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
protons and Ca2+ compete for binding to surface charge and the selectivity filter, but that Ca2+ also competes with protons for the activation pathway of the channel.

extracellular protons and Ca2+ interact at several sites on the T-type channel, which are not necessarily located in the same region of the protein, and that these interactions modify the gating and permeation properties of the channel in a complex manner.

extracellular protons and Ca2+ interact in a complex manner with the T-type channel, with both cation species competing for surface charges and the selectivity filter, and Ca2+ modulating proton effects on gating.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protons and Ca2+ interact in the extracellular space of the CaV3.1 channel, and the interaction of these two ions is crucial for the regulation of channel function.
extracellular protons interact with CaV3.1 channels in a Ca2+ concentration–dependent manner, with the proton effects being modulated by extracytoplasmic Ca2+ and other monovalent cation species.
Ca2+ is the main competitor of protons in the modulation of the T-type channel function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ and protons can act as modulators of T-type Ca2+-channel function.

the modulation of T-type Ca2+-channel function by protons is not only dependent on the proton concentration and the voltage dependence of channel activation but also on the concentration of Ca2+ and monovalent cation in the external solution.
the effects of proton are complex and depend on the concentration of Ca2+ and on the permeation properties of the channel.
